what_its_for: Cefaclor is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections such as ear infections, throat infections (like strep throat), sinus infections, urinary tract infections, skin infections, and certain lung infections like bronchitis or pneumonia. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It will NOT work for colds, flu, or other viral infections.
how_to_take: Take cefaclor exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Swallow capsules whole with a full glass of water. If you have the chewable tablet, chew it completely before swallowing. If you have the liquid suspension, shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring spoon or syringe that comes with the medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Always finish the full course of treatment even if you start feeling better, to make sure the infection is completely cleared.
dosing: The dose depends on your age, weight, and the type of infection being treated. Adults are typically prescribed 250 mg to 500 mg every 8 hours (three times a day) or every 12 hours (twice a day) for 7 to 14 days. Children's doses are based on body weight and are determined by the doctor. Always follow the specific instructions on your prescription label. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this could increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store capsules and tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture — do not store in the bathroom. Store the liquid suspension in the refrigerator after mixing and use it within 14 days — throw away any leftover liquid after 14 days. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping doses or stopping treatment early, even if you feel better — this can allow the bacteria to return or become resistant to antibiotics. Tell your doctor before taking antacids, as some may affect how cefaclor is absorbed. Avoid drinking alcohol while on antibiotics as it can worsen side effects like stomach upset. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have similar symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: a severe skin rash, hives, or blistering; swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing or swallowing (signs of a serious allergic reaction); severe or persistent diarrhea, especially if it is watery or bloody (this could be a sign of a serious intestinal infection called C. difficile); yellowing of the skin or eyes; dark urine; unusual bruising or bleeding; or if your symptoms are not improving after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting cefaclor. However, it is very important to keep taking the full course of antibiotics as prescribed, even if your symptoms improve. Stopping early may cause your infection to come back or make it harder to treat in the future.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may adjust your dose. Make sure to tell your doctor about any kidney conditions. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Cefaclor is generally considered safe during pregnancy, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Small amounts pass into breast milk, so discuss with your doctor before breastfeeding. Elderly patients: Older adults may need a lower dose if they have reduced kidney function — your doctor will decide the right dose for you. Children: Cefaclor can be used in infants and children — the dose is carefully calculated by the doctor based on your child's weight. Penicillin allergy: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to penicillin, as there is a small chance you could also be allergic to cefaclor.
